summary: Discusses the interfaces group of MIB-II and the experience gained from many media-specific MIB modules. It clarifies and extends how network interfaces are described for management. It is on the standards track at the draft standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2863 defines SNMP data for describing network interfaces and their condition. It represents interface layers separately and adds ways to report fast links and changing interface states.

questions: what is the interfaces group mib
subtitle: How SNMP describes network interfaces, their layers, counters, and operational state.

tldr.problem: The earlier interface model could not clearly represent layered interfaces, changing interfaces, and counters or speeds that exceeded its original limits.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2863 gives each interface sub-layer a row, records layer relationships in the ifStackTable, and adds high-capacity counters, speed reporting, names, and operational states.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2863 obsoletes RFC 2233. It is a Draft Standard that has been updated by RFC 8892.

today: RFC 2863 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2233. It has been updated by RFC 8892.

sections.title: A Common Interface Model
sections.content:
The Interfaces Group MIB defines managed objects for network interfaces. It extends the general interface group in MIB-II and incorporates earlier extensions, drawing on experience from media-specific MIB modules.

The general objects let management software inspect different kinds of interfaces in a consistent way. A media-specific MIB can add details for a particular medium, while this RFC clarifies how the general model represents interfaces and their sub-layers.

RFC 2863 replaces RFC 2233. The module is written for SMIv2, the language used to define SNMP management information.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB gives management software a shared set of facts about network interfaces. Other MIB modules can add details for a specific kind of interface.

sections.title: Interfaces Can Have Multiple Layers
sections.content:
A network interface may consist of several sub-layers, each with its own technology and management details. For example, PPP can run over an HDLC link connected through an RS-232-like interface.

RFC 2863 represents each sub-layer with its own row in ifTable. The ifStackTable records which rows are above or below others. This structure can describe both one upper layer using several lower layers and several upper layers sharing a lower layer.

Packet counters are measured at each layer in relation to the next higher layer or forwarding function. The RFC recommends keeping the number of rows to what network management needs and asks media-specific MIB designers to explain their layer model.
sections.plainLanguage: A single connection can contain several interface layers. Each layer gets its own management entry, and another table records how the entries connect.

sections.title: The Four Tables
sections.content:
The MIB contains four tables. ifTable holds the basic interface entries. ifXTable holds additional and replacement objects, including objects brought in from the earlier extension table.

ifStackTable describes relationships among interface sub-layers. ifRcvAddressTable lists media-level addresses an interface receives. Designers of media-specific MIBs must explain how that address table applies to their technology.

Not every object applies to every interface type. Instead of splitting the original table and requiring broad changes to SNMP agents, the RFC defines compliance groups for objects that apply to all, packet-oriented, or fixed-length and character-oriented interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB separates basic interface details, extra details, layer relationships, and receive addresses into four tables. Compliance groups identify which objects apply to each interface type.

sections.title: Interface Numbers and Names
sections.content:
Each interface has an ifIndex that stays stable between network-management-system re-initializations. RFC 2863 removes the old rule that an index must be no greater than ifNumber. This permits gaps in index values when interfaces are added or removed; ifNumber still reports the number of interfaces.

An index used by a removed interface must not be assigned to a different interface before the next re-initialization. The RFC adds ifCounterDiscontinuityTime so managers can detect when counters reset without changing the index.

ifName contains the device's local name for an interface. ifAlias lets a manager assign a non-volatile name that must survive reboots, while ifDescr remains a description.
sections.plainLanguage: An interface keeps its management number while it exists, even if numbers are not consecutive. Separate name fields provide the device's name and a manager-assigned name that survives reboots.

sections.title: Counters and Link Speed
sections.content:
A 32-bit counter can wrap quickly on a fast link. The RFC adds 64-bit high-capacity counters while retaining the original 32-bit counters, which report the low 32 bits when the larger counters are used.

At or below 20,000,000 bits per second, 32-bit byte and packet counters must be supported. Above that rate and below 650,000,000 bits per second, implementations must support 64-bit octet counters and 32-bit packet counters. At 650,000,000 bits per second or faster, both counter types must be 64-bit.

The older ifSpeed field cannot report above (2**31)-1 bits per second. The new ifHighSpeed reports in units of 1,000,000 bits per second.
sections.plainLanguage: Fast links can make small counters wrap before a manager reads them. The RFC requires larger counters at higher speeds and adds a speed field for links beyond the older field's range.

sections.title: Operational States and Link Traps
sections.content:
The ifOperStatus values include dormant for an interface waiting for an external event, notPresent when a component is missing, and lowerLayerDown when a lower interface is down. If administrative status is not down but operational status is down, the RFC says a fault is presumed.

For an interface above other layers, status can be up when a lower layer can pass packets. It is lowerLayerDown when all lower layers are down, missing, lower-layer-down, or testing.

Link-up and link-down traps track transitions into or out of down, except transitions to or from notPresent. Managers can control which sub-layers generate traps, and agents should limit trap rates when a link repeatedly changes state.
sections.plainLanguage: The status values distinguish a fault from an interface waiting for something or missing hardware. Link alerts report meaningful changes without treating hardware removal as an ordinary link failure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some MIB objects can be changed or created. Unauthorized changes could disable interfaces or create unwanted connectivity, affecting network operation.

The RFC says SNMPv1 alone does not control who may read or change these objects, even on a protected network. It recommends considering SNMPv3 security and access-control features, and leaves correct access configuration to the customer or user.
sections.plainLanguage: Some interface information can be changed, so access must be limited to authorized users. The RFC recommends using SNMPv3 security and access controls.
